Steps in Character Creation

Choose an alignment, roll six ability scores in order, select a class that satisfies the prime requisite, then record hit points, armor class, saving throws, starting equipment and languages. Strength, Intelligence, Wisdom, Dexterity, Constitution and Charisma are scored from 3 to 18; the normal modifier is -3 at 3, -2 at 4-5, -1 at 6-8, none at 9-12, +1 at 13-15, +2 at 16-17 and +3 at 18. Clerics and druids use Wisdom, fighters and dwarves Strength, magic-users Intelligence, thieves Dexterity, and mystics Strength (with Dexterity and Wisdom 13+ to qualify). A prime requisite of 13-15 grants +5% XP and 16-18 grants +10%; 6-8 gives -10% and 3-5 gives -20% (mystics: -5% and -10%). Elves need Strength 13+ plus Intelligence 13+ for +5%, or Intelligence 16+ for +10%; halflings need Strength or Dexterity 13+ for +5%, or both for +10%.

Starting hit points are the maximum of the class hit die plus the Constitution adjustment; subsequent levels roll the hit die, with a minimum of 1 point. Starting gold is 3d6 x 10 gp. Characters begin with a languages score based on Intelligence and buy equipment from the Equipment chapter.

The Character Classes

Choose one class. A human may reach level 36 as a fighter, cleric, magic-user or thief; demihumans have lower maximum levels and class restrictions. A class supplies hit dice, attack progression, saving throws, experience requirements, spell access and special abilities.

Coins weigh 10 per pound (100 cn), gems and jewels are carried separately, and each item has a cost in gold pieces and a weight in coin weight. Armor class is descending: unarmored AC 9, leather 7, scale 6, chain 5, banded 4, plate 3 and full plate 0. A shield subtracts 1 from AC.

Other Character Abilities

Weapon Mastery is optional. Humans receive weapon choices by level; demihumans begin with Basic skill in class-approved weapons. The five ranks are Basic, Skilled, Expert, Master and Grand Master. Each rank improves damage, range, attack bonus, defense or special effects as shown in the Weapon Mastery journal.

The optional General Skills system lets a character choose noncombat skills. Every 1st-level character starts with four blank slots; Intelligence 13-15 grants one extra slot, 16-17 grants two and 18 grants three. A slot is spent when a skill is chosen. Art may be based on Intelligence or Wisdom; skills marked "choose type" record the player's specialty on the sheet.

Movement

Exploration movement is measured in turns (10 minutes) and dungeon movement in rounds. Encumbered characters move more slowly; the movement rate is derived from total carried weight. Running increases speed but makes stealth impossible and can cause fatigue.

Normal speed is measured in feet per turn and includes mapping, resting and peeking around corners. Encounter speed is one third of normal speed per round; running speed equals the normal speed in feet per round and can be maintained for at most 30 rounds before exhaustion. Outdoor movement is tripled (feet become yards). Groups move at the rate of the slowest member.

Water and air travel use their own tables for ships, rowing and flying speeds; weather and currents modify travel time.

Encounters and Evasion

Checklist: switch from 10-minute turns to 10-second rounds; both sides roll 1d6 for surprise (1-2 means surprised); if neither side is surprised both roll 1d6 for initiative, while a surprised side loses initiative automatically; roll reactions if the DM does not already know them; resolve the results; then assume at least one full turn has passed.

Chance of encounter: in a dungeon or city, roll 1d6 every two turns and 1d12 once at night, with an encounter on a 1. In the wilderness, roll 1d6 by day and 1d12 at night: clear, grasslands, inhabited or settled land needs a 1; forest, river, hills, barren land, desert, ocean or aerial needs 1-2; swamp, jungle or mountains needs 1-3.

Surprise: each side rolls 1d6; a 1 or 2 means that side is surprised. If both sides are surprised both lose one round. If one side is surprised, it loses initiative and the other side gains a free round or automatic evasion. If neither is surprised there is no advantage.

Distance: surprise replaces the normal distance with 1d4 x 10 feet or yards; when only one side is surprised it notices at that distance and the surprised side notices at half. Otherwise consult the Encounter Distances Table: dungeon bright light 4d6 x 10 ft, dim light 2d6 x 10 ft, no light 1d4 x 10 ft; wilderness bright 4d6 x 10 yards, dim 2d6 x 10 yards, poor visibility 1d4 x 10 yards; undersea 1d6 x 10 yards.

Monster reactions: roll 2d6 on the Monster Reactions (2d6) table in the BECMI Tables compendium:

2d6Reaction
2-3Monster attacks
4-6Monster is aggressive (growls, threatens); roll again in one round with a penalty of -4 to the roll
7-9Monster is cautious; roll again in one round
10-11Monster is neutral; roll again in one round with a bonus of +4 to the roll
12Monster is friendly

The first roll ignores Charisma. Later rolls apply the speaker's Charisma modifier plus PC actions from a -2 penalty to a +2 bonus and the modifier carried by the previous result. Never roll more than three times; if the third roll is below 10, the monster attacks or leaves.

Evasion and pursuit: an unsurprised group can evade a surprised group automatically. Otherwise the DM rolls d100 against the Evasion Table by party size and number of monsters, adjusted for terrain, relative speed and scouts, with a minimum 5% chance. A failed roll starts a chase: both sides roll 1d6 for initiative each round, and monsters check morale every five rounds.

Settled and castle terrain: a "Castle" result uses Wilderness Subtable 10: Castle Encounters (1d6) in the BECMI Tables compendium. Roll 1d6 for the owner's class, 1d20+8 for level (demihumans have fixed levels), and a second 1d6 for alignment: 1 Chaotic, 2-4 Neutral, 5-6 Lawful. Patrol size and reaction are by class: fighter 2-12 heavy horsemen (pursue on 1-3), magic-user 2-12 heavy footmen (pursue on 1), cleric 2-12 medium horsemen (pursue on 1-2), demihuman 2-12 demihumans (pursue on 1); the remaining results are Ignore or Friendly.

City terrain: a "Special" result uses Wilderness Subtable 11: City Encounters (1d20). First roll 1d8 to select one of its eight sections, then roll 1d20 in that section for the city-dweller; level and intent are for the DM to decide. The same table can be used to pick a location by translating the profession (a judge suggests a courtroom, an undertaker a cemetery).

Combat

Each round: roll initiative (1d6 per side), resolve morale, movement, missile fire, spells and hand-to-hand attacks in order. To hit, roll d20 and compare the result to the attack matrix using THAC0 and the target's descending AC; a natural 1 always misses and a natural 20 always hits. Damage is rolled after a hit, modified by Strength for melee weapons.

Mass Combat

For battles with many combatants, the War Machine converts each unit into a Combat Result using troop class, hit dice, morale and leaders. Opposing results are compared on the War Machine table to produce casualties, gains and losses. The Siege Machine resolves attacks on fortifications using class, armor and construction factors.

Leaders add their level and ability bonuses; terrain, surprise and morale can shift the result. The system resolves the battle as a whole rather than individual attacks.

Experience

XP comes from five sources: exceptional role-playing, party goals, defeated monsters, treasure kept, and exceptional actions. Monster XP is the sum of each monster's XP value multiplied by its count, divided among every PC and NPC who participated; a failed fight earns one quarter. Treasure is worth 1 XP per gp value won and kept (thieves also earn XP from money stolen); salaries for ordinary jobs do not count. Selling a magical item earns at most 10% of its creation cost in XP, not its full sale price.

Exceptional role-playing, exceptional actions and exceptional skill use are each worth 1/20 of the base XP needed for the character's next level; only one role-playing bonus is awarded per game session. A goal bonus is normally equal to the monster XP earned during that storyline. Unless the DM rules otherwise, prime requisite modifiers apply to all XP earned.

A character can gain at most one level per adventure. XP beyond that is retained only up to one point below the threshold for the second level ahead; the rest is lost. Mystics gain treasure XP only when it is donated to the needy and must tithe 10% of treasure to their cloister; acrobatic mystics take an extra -20% to all XP.

Nonplayer Characters

Retainers and mercenaries are hired with pay, food and lodging. Their loyalty depends on the employer's Charisma, alignment, treatment and regular pay. Specialists such as sages, smiths and alchemists charge for services and may require contracts or advances.

Hirelings have morale scores and abandon or betray an employer when morale fails. The DM controls all NPC decisions, even when the players negotiate terms.

Strongholds and Dominions

A character can build a stronghold after reaching the appropriate level. Construction cost depends on size, materials and fortifications; monthly upkeep covers wages, supplies and repairs. Staff are hired from the NPC rules and have morale and loyalty.

A dominion generates income from taxes, trade and resources. The ruler must maintain order, collect taxes and defend the territory; population and attitude affect revenue.

Dungeon Master Procedures

When no specific rule applies, the DM sets a target number on d20 (easy 5, moderate 10, hard 15, very hard 20) and applies the relevant ability adjustment. Ability checks are optional; a natural 20 succeeds and a natural 1 fails when the DM uses that convention.

Aging modifies ability scores at thresholds determined by the DM. Alignment changes require a major shift in behavior and may cause the loss of class abilities. Anti-magic areas suppress spells and magical item powers. The DM's final ruling resolves ambiguous cases.

Monsters

Each monster entry lists armor class, hit dice, hit points, number appearing, movement, attacks, damage, special abilities, morale, treasure type and XP value. Hit dice are d8; a "+" adds hit points without changing the HD for attack or saving throw purposes.

Monsters use the same descending AC and saving throw categories as characters. Special attacks such as breath weapons, poison, paralysis and charm usually allow a saving throw with a stated modifier. Treasure type determines the rolled treasure.

Immortals

Immortal characters use spheres (matter, energy, time, space and thought) and ranks from novice to Hierophant. Each rank grants powers, higher ability scores and increased hit points, while requiring experience and a patron's approval.

Mortals may qualify through the paths of the Dynamism, the Hierarchy or the Void, each with different prerequisites. Immortal magic uses the same level structure but much larger energy costs.

Treasure

Treasure is generated by lettered types that specify coins, gems, jewelry and magical items. Gold, electrum, silver, copper and platinum have different values; gems and jewelry are valued individually and weigh less than coins.

Use the Treasure tab on any sheet to roll a lettered type, a gem or jewelry value, or a magical item. Chance entries are d100 rolls of the number shown or less; lair coins are multiplied by 1,000 and carried coins are individual pieces. Gems and jewelry use separate d100 value tables, lowered by 10 for parties below level 9.

Magical items include potions, scrolls, rings, wands, staves, swords, armor and miscellaneous items; roll on the main table, then on the matching subtable. Missile talents such as speaking, stunning, teleporting, transporting and wounding are separate from ordinary item powers. Creating an item costs gold and spell levels and requires a roll for success.

Magical Item Creation

Only characters able to cast spells can create magical items. With the exception of item restrictions, these formulas apply to clerics and druids by substituting Wisdom for Intelligence in every calculation.

Enchantment chance: roll d100 against ([ Intelligence + Level ] x 2) - (3 x spell level). For an armor or weapon bonus, substitute the number of pluses or minuses for the spell level. The character succeeds on a roll equal to or less than that chance. A failed roll ruins the gold, time and components already spent.

Armor and weapons: multiply the nonmagical price in gp by its encumbrance in cn, then divide by 3 for armor or a shield and round up to the next 10 gp. Each plus or minus costs another base price, with a minimum of 3,000 gp for armor or a shield and 100 gp for a weapon. Bonuses effective only against a particular opponent cost half a base per plus, reduced by 10% per restriction. The maximum bonus is +5 or -5.

Spell effects: each spell level costs 1,000 gp. charges add 10% of the initial cost each; permanency costs five times the initial cost (equivalent to 50 charges). Each restriction reduces the spell-effect cost by 10%; a nonrechargeable item costs 20% less. An item usable only once per hour, day, week or month costs 20%, 25%, 30% or 35% less, then includes 30 charges plus one charge for each use allowed in that period.

Construction time: one week plus one day for every 1,000 gp of enchantment cost, rounded up. A 14,000 gp item therefore takes 21 days by the printed rule, even though the book's worked example states 31 days; the DM should resolve that inconsistency before play.

Magical constructs: creation costs 2,000 gp per Hit Die plus 5,000 gp per asterisk, requires at least 18th level and the create magical monsters spell, and rolls ([ Intelligence + Level ] x 2) - (HD + asterisks). Three asterisks require create any monster, which clerics cannot cast. A construct cannot exceed 36 HD.

Spell research: a spell costs 1,000 gp per level and uses the standard enchantment timetable. Common spells subtract 3 per level from the chance, new spells 5; each failed attempt grants a cumulative +5% on the following roll, but a roll of 95 or higher always fails and there is no automatic success.

Experience: at the DM's discretion, successful first-time creation grants XP equal to the gp spent. A successful vase, house or giant-sized magical construction grants one third of the gp spent instead. Repeat work grants no XP.

Campaigning

A campaign links adventures into a continuing world. The DM prepares key locations, factions, rumors and encounters, then adapts them to player choices. Consistent timekeeping, geography and NPC memory make the setting believable.

Use wandering monsters, random treasure and reaction checks sparingly so that the story remains coherent. Reward clever plans as well as combat, and let character actions change the world.

The Planes of Existence

The Prime Plane is the balanced home world of ordinary adventurers. Other planes are arranged around it: the Ethereal Plane overlays the Prime, the four Elemental Planes connect to it through wormholes, and the Outer Planes lie beyond them. Interplanar travel normally passes through the Ethereal Plane, because direct travel between the Prime and the elemental spheres is not available to ordinary characters.

In the Ethereal Plane ether appears as gray fog. Light works normally but illuminates only the ether; infravision is nearly useless because everything shares the same temperature. Visitors can breathe, cannot fall, and cannot walk. Movement requires magic and changes with the material nearby on the Prime Plane: vacuum doubles speed, air is normal, fire or water reduces it to three quarters, soil or wood to half, rock to one quarter, and metal or lead stops movement entirely.

Elemental planes are hostile environments. Air dominates Water, Water dominates Fire, Fire dominates Earth, and Earth dominates Air; Air and Fire oppose each other, as do Earth and Water. Survival requires spells such as create air or survival, a ring of elemental adaptation, or a talisman of elemental travel. Energy-based effects work normally; matter-based effects may be altered or negated.

The Outer Planes are the realms of alignment, deities and immortal powers. They are reached by advanced magic or immortal travel. Beyond the multiverse lies whatever the DM places there; use the same plane rules as a frontier rather than assuming fixed physics.

Variant Rules

These options are optional. Apply them consistently or not at all, since they change encounters, advancement and combat pacing.

Ability scores and saving throws: in the standard game only Wisdom modifies saves versus spells. The DM may also apply the ability modifier to the matching category: Strength vs. paralysis and petrification, Intelligence vs. mind attacks, Wisdom vs. spells, Dexterity vs. wands and breath weapons, and Constitution vs. poison but not death rays. Charisma gives no save bonus. A combined modifier cannot exceed +3 or -3.

Death in the campaign: resurrection magic can be removed to make death final. A gentler option keeps a character at 0 hit points unconscious and mortally wounded: roll a saving throw versus death ray each round while taking damage and once per ten minutes; failure means death. Healing magic or a successful Healing skill check with a -5 penalty stabilizes the character.

Demihuman and mystic advancement: the standard caps keep these classes balanced because they begin with many abilities. The extended table lets them reach level 36. Under that option demihumans use the normal attack chart instead of Attack Ranks: dwarves attack as fighters, elves and halflings as clerics; mystics attack as fighters. Hit points above 9th level become fixed, saving throws stop improving at the old cap, and spell access follows the normal spell table for casters.

Nonlethal combat: divide each damage roll into real damage (one quarter, rounded down) and nonlethal damage (the remainder). Track them separately. When their sum reaches the target's hit points, the target falls unconscious. Nonlethal damage wears off in two stages of 2d6 x 10 minutes; real damage only heals normally. Unarmed attacks and purpose-built practice weapons have no penalty; using an ordinary weapon to deal nonlethal damage imposes a -3 attack penalty.

Appendix 1 — The D&D Game World

The Rules Cyclopedia presents two linked campaign settings on the planet Mystara. The Known World is the surface setting where most characters begin: kingdoms, city-states and frontier wilderness suitable for low- and mid-level play. The Hollow World is a vast interior world reached through special passes; it preserves ancient cultures, dinosaur-hunting grounds and immortal guardians, and suits higher-level exploration.

Use the Known World for a conventional dungeon-and-domain campaign. Introduce the Hollow World when the party is ready for polar openings, longer journeys and immortal politics. Nothing in the system requires either setting; the compendia provide the rules, while the DM supplies geography, factions and rumors.

Encounters and Reaction Rolls

Chance of encounter: in a dungeon or city, roll 1d6 every two turns (1d12 once at night); on a 1 an encounter occurs. In the wilderness, roll 1d6 by day and 1d12 at night: clear, grasslands, inhabited or settled land needs a 1; forest, river, hills, barren land, desert, ocean or aerial needs 1-2; swamp, jungle or mountains needs 1-3.

Surprise: both sides roll 1d6; a 1 or 2 means surprised. Both surprised loses a round for each side; one surprised gives the other a free round or automatic evasion; neither surprised gives no advantage. Surprise sets distance to 1d4 x 10 feet or yards, with the surprised side noticing at half distance when only one side is surprised.

Distance: without surprise, dungeon bright light is 4d6 x 10 ft, dim light 2d6 x 10 ft, darkness 1d4 x 10 ft; wilderness bright daylight 4d6 x 10 yards, dim light 2d6 x 10 yards, very poor visibility 1d4 x 10 yards. Ocean ships are detected at 300/120/40 yards by visibility and ocean monsters use 4d6/2d6/1d4 x 10 yards; undersea uses 1d6 x 10 yards. Wandering monsters in a dungeon appear 2d6 x 10 ft away.

Reactions: roll 2d6 on the Monster Reactions (2d6) table in the BECMI Tables compendium: 2-3 Monster attacks; 4-6 the monster is aggressive and you roll again in one round with a penalty of -4; 7-9 the monster is cautious and you roll again; 10-11 the monster is neutral and you roll again with a bonus of +4; 12 the monster is friendly. The first roll ignores Charisma; later rolls add Charisma, PC actions of -2 to +2 and the listed modifier. Never roll more than three times; a third roll below 10 means the monster attacks or leaves.

Which monsters: roll 1d20 on the Dungeon Encounters table for the current dungeon level, then roll the number appearing shown in that row. In the wilderness, roll 1d8 for the terrain column, then 1d12 on the indicated subtable. The two special results are rollable too: Wilderness Subtable 10: Castle Encounters (1d6) gives the castle owner's class, 1d20+8 level and alignment (second 1d6: 1 Chaotic, 2-4 Neutral, 5-6 Lawful), and Wilderness Subtable 11: City Encounters (1d20) needs a 1d8 to choose a section first. All eleven wilderness subtables and the six dungeon tables are in the BECMI Tables compendium.

Evasion and pursuit: compare party size to the number of monsters on the Evasion Table, then apply terrain, speed and scout adjustments with a minimum 5% chance. Pursuit uses 1d6 initiative per side each round and a morale check every five rounds.

Magic item creation: the chance of success is a d100 roll against ([Intelligence or Wisdom + level] x 2) - (3 x spell level), or the number of bonuses for armor and weapons. Costs and time are calculated from the checklists in the Enchantment rules; they are not a random table.

Weapon Mastery (Optional)

Weapon mastery lets a character study one weapon in depth, or several weapons less intensely. It is optional: the DM decides whether to use it. All characters, not only fighters, can learn it.

With these rules a human starts with no weapon skill and receives weapon choices. Demihumans start with Basic skill in all weapons allowed to their class, but do not gain weapon choices; they improve through training at levels 4, 8 and 12 (dwarves) and after maximum level.

A weapon choice buys one weapon used in one fashion. A bastard sword used one-handed and the same sword used two-handed are two separate choices. The net is a single exception.

Condensed reference from Rules Cyclopedia, Chapter 5.
